« Même avant que je sois né, ils parlaie: “Even before I was born, they were already talking about solutions” – Why are responses to police racism struggling to take hold?
Moratoire, commission d’enquête, définan: Moratorium, commission of inquiry, defunding: solutions to police racism exist. Why do they remain blocked?
Cercle de dialogue tenu dans les locaux: A dialogue circle held at the Coalition Pozé offices during the evening “How do we counter police brutality?”, organized by La Converse, the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel, the Coalition Pozé and the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel. Photo: Thomas Bourgoin.
Cet article est né dans la foulée du sca: This article was born in the wake of the scandal at Montréal-Nord’s neighbourhood police station 39. The allegations of racism and discrimination within the SPVM, and the reactions they provoked in the affected neighbourhoods, quickly caught our attention.
À <em>La Converse</em>, nous nous intére: At La Converse, we are less interested in one-off controversies than in what they reveal about the realities communities live. After covering the press conference held in Montréal-Nord and the demonstration that followed, we noticed that one question kept coming up: what do we do now?
C’est dans cet esprit que nous avons org: It was in that spirit that we organized a dialogue evening at the Coalition Pozé headquarters in Anjou. For more than four hours, young people, community workers, researchers, activists, lawyers and residents discussed police violence, racial profiling and ways to fight them.
Au départ, je pensais produire un compte: At first, I planned to write a report on the gathering. But as the discussions went on, another question took hold: is it really solutions that are lacking, or is it the obstacles to putting them into practice that explain why they have had no effect?
Pour répondre à cette question, j’ai réé: To answer that question, I listened again to the entire evening, conducted additional interviews, then went through several reports, research studies and public data on police stops and oversight mechanisms.
Cet article ne prétend pas clore le déba: This article does not claim to close the debate. Rather, it seeks to understand why solutions that have sometimes been called for over decades still struggle to materialize, and why the strategies for bringing about change are themselves still debated.
<strong>Moratoire sur les interpellation: Moratorium on police stops, public commission of inquiry, defunding the police, stronger oversight mechanisms: solutions to police racism are numerous – and sometimes long-standing. Gathered in Anjou for a dialogue evening organized by La Converse, young people, activists, researchers and community workers mostly asked about the obstacles standing in the way of putting them into practice, including institutional resistance and sometimes diverging visions of change.
« Même avant que je sois né, ils parlaie: “Even before I was born, they were already talking about solutions. I’m sure that when my grandchildren are born, they’ll still be talking about solutions!” By the time Julian Grau-Brown speaks, the evening organized by La Converse at the Coalition Pozé headquarters is well underway. A social worker and doctoral student at McGill University, he expresses a weariness that goes beyond his own generation: that of communities that, for decades, have seen the same findings about racism within the Montréal police come back, and the same recommendations, without the hoped-for changes ever materializing.
Pendant plusieurs heures, les participan: For several hours, the participants at our evening discussed police racism in Montréal. The solutions raised are many: a moratorium on police stops, a public commission of inquiry, defunding the police, funding community organizations, reinvesting in neighbourhoods, and more. So many that one question gradually took over: are we really short of solutions, or are the obstacles to applying them what explain why they have had no effect?
Cette interrogation traverse plusieurs d: That question runs through many of the exchanges at the dialogue evening organized by La Converse in the wake of the scandal at Montréal-Nord’s neighbourhood police station 39. Because although participants don’t always agree on the means to advocate (some defending institutional reforms, others a break with the system or a show of force), many nonetheless share the same finding: police racism is not a series of isolated incidents but a systemic problem whose remedies remain largely up in the air.
<strong>Moratoire : une solution déjà su: Moratorium: a solution already on the table
Lorsque les participants de la soirée on: When the evening’s participants were invited to propose solutions, several expressed a kind of weariness at how unfinished the solutions remain. The example of the moratorium on police stops illustrates this feeling well.
Depuis plusieurs années, les chercheurs: For several years, researchers have documented the significant disparities affecting Black, Arab and Indigenous people in police stops in Montréal. A first report published in 2019 already concluded that Black people were far more likely to be stopped than white people. In response to that study, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) adopted a new policy on police stops in 2021.
Puis, un second mandat confié à quatre c: Then a second mandate, entrusted to four independent researchers, set out to assess the effects of that reform. Submitted in June 2023, their <l1>report</l1> concludes that racial profiling persists and that the changes adopted did not produce the hoped-for results.
Les chercheurs Mariam Hassaoui, Victor A: Researchers Mariam Hassaoui, Victor Armony, Alicia Boatswain-Kyte and Massimiliano Mulone make only one recommendation: suspend stops that are linked neither to a criminal investigation nor to reasonable suspicion. In other words, impose a moratorium on so-called routine stops.
Le directeur du SPVM,<l1> Fady Dagher, r: SPVM director<l1> Fady Dagher, however, rejected this recommendation</l1>. He said at the time that a moratorium would be a “symbolic measure” and maintained that he preferred to focus on a change of culture within the police force itself.
Cette décision provoque une vive réactio: The decision provoked a strong reaction among several organizations and researchers. In December 2024, at a <l1>consultation before Montréal’s Commission de la sécurité publique</l1>, several of them denounced the SPVM’s refusal to apply the one recommendation made by the scientific team. “Why did the SPVM commission a research report from independent experts if it had no intention whatsoever of following their one and only recommendation?” asked Lynda Khelil of the Ligue des droits et libertés.
Enfin, en septembre 2024, la juge Domini: Finally, in September 2024, Justice Dominique Poulin of the Quebec Superior Court handed down a historic ruling, concluding that racial profiling is systemic within the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM).
Pour plusieurs participants de la soirée: For several participants at the La Converse evening, this episode perfectly illustrates the sense of powerlessness that runs through communities affected by racial profiling. For them, the moratorium has become much more than a technical measure: it is a test of institutions’ ability to apply the changes they themselves commissioned and documented.
Pour Massimiliano Mulone, l’une des limi: For Massimiliano Mulone, one of the system’s limits has less to do with a lack of recourse than with how accessible it is. “People know very little about the recourses they have,” says the researcher, who believes the mechanisms for overseeing the police remain largely unknown to the public.
Le Commissaire à la déontologie policièr: The Police Ethics Commissioner, responsible for receiving complaints about police conduct, and the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), which steps in notably in cases of death or serious injury linked to a police intervention, remain little known among citizens.
Selon M. Mulone, les organismes chargés: According to Mr. Mulone, the bodies responsible for this oversight also operate with limited resources, up against far more powerful police institutions. “The bodies responsible for handling citizens’ complaints are already completely overwhelmed,” he says in an interview with La Converse.
Le chercheur souligne l’écart entre les: The researcher points to the gap between the resources available to the SPVM, whose budget is approaching a billion dollars, and those of the institutions responsible for external oversight. For him, this imbalance helps fuel the sense of powerlessness expressed by several participants at the evening. The mechanisms exist, but they remain hard for many families to understand, use or get through.
L’<l1>affaire David Kalubi</l1> illustre: According to Massimiliano Mulone, the <l1>David Kalubi case</l1> illustrates certain limits of the oversight mechanisms. The young man died in 2017, at age 23, after being arrested by police and held at the Montréal courthouse. The family did not know at the time that a police ethics complaint could be filed.
C’est l’intervention du militant Alexand: It was the intervention of activist Alexandre Popovic of the Coalition contre la répression et les abus policiers (CRAP) that made it possible for a complaint to be filed before the limitation period expired.
Cet épisode soulève, selon M. Mulone, un: According to Mr. Mulone, this episode raises a broader question: what happens in situations where no one knows the available recourse, or no one accompanies loved ones through the process? The example also shows that the oversight mechanisms sometimes rely on the work of organizations, activists or citizens who understand these complex procedures. Without that expertise, some families risk never gaining access to the recourse provided by law.
Pour plusieurs acteurs réunis à Anjou, c: For several of those gathered in Anjou, this reality also feeds distrust of institutions: the tools exist, but access to them remains unequal and often depends on resources outside the public bodies themselves.
<strong>C-37 et une commission pour alle: C-37 and a commission to go further
Parmi les solutions évoquées lors de la: Among the solutions raised during the evening, one comes up regularly: the creation of a public commission of inquiry into police racism and profiling.
Pour l’avocate Dardia Joseph, également: For lawyer Dardia Joseph, who is also deputy director of the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel, this demand is anything but symbolic; it responds squarely to the limits of the current mechanisms. “The mechanisms for overseeing police action, as we have them right now, have shown an effectiveness that is, all things considered, fairly limited,” she observes in an interview.
Elle rappelle notamment que les plaintes: She points out in particular that complaints of racial profiling rarely lead to sanctions. According to recent data from the Police Ethics Commissioner cited by the lawyer, 493 complaints of racial profiling were filed from 2024 to 2025. Only six of them resulted in a citation before the Police Ethics Tribunal, and barely two ended in a decision finding an ethics breach. For M<sup>e</sup> Joseph, these figures illustrate the limits of the current police oversight mechanisms and explain why several groups are calling for more powerful investigative tools.
Récemment, le ministre de la Sécurité pu: Recently, Public Security Minister Ian Lafrenière appointed an independent observer to follow the internal investigation into the Montréal-Nord police station 39 affair. It is an initiative that does not satisfy participants at the dialogue evening, because “an independent observer is not a commission of inquiry,” M<sup>e</sup> Joseph reminds us.
La commission d’enquête publique qu’elle: The public commission of inquiry she is advocating would be held under the <l1>Act respecting public inquiry commissions (C-37)</l1>. “It’s really important to specify ‘under C-37’ because it’s precisely when public commissions of inquiry are held under that law that they come with the powers that seem valuable to us for getting to the bottom of things, for tackling the issue in a fullness we didn’t have before,” she explains. And it would be a first in Quebec on the subject of racial profiling, the legal expert goes on.
Selon elle, une telle commission permett: According to her, such a commission would also make it possible to obtain documents, impose greater transparency and give a place to the associations and organizations concerned. “It allows them to be a party to that commission of inquiry, to question and cross-examine witnesses,” she adds.
L’avocate insiste toutefois sur le fait: The lawyer insists, however, that a commission would not be a miracle cure. “I’m not here to promote a solution as if it were perfect,” she says, “because the public commission of inquiry is not a panacea.” That said, she acknowledges its important “expressive value”: that of publicly recognizing lived experiences and making racial profiling a matter of collective interest rather than a collection of individual cases.
Pour le travailleur social Julian Grau-B: For social worker Julian Grau-Brown, the solution lies along another path: police powers must be reduced and resources reinvested elsewhere. The young activist champions the idea of defunding the police, a proposal that remains a minority view in public debate but finds an echo among some participants at the evening.
Selon lui, certaines réformes peinent à: According to him, some reforms struggle to produce change because they leave intact the place the police institution occupies. In his eyes, the moratorium on police stops is a concrete example. “It’s something that would reduce police officers’ power,” he explains. He points out that a police stop occurs when an officer approaches a person in a park, on the street or in front of a school to obtain information or identify them when no offence has been committed.
Pour Julian, la récente ouverture de la: For Julian, the recent openness of Montréal Mayor Soraya Martinez-Ferrada to a moratorium is “a victory worth celebrating.” But he believes the debate must also address the place police occupy in responding to social problems. He argues that the defunding proposal aims to shift part of the resources to community organizations, local services and social interventions. In his view, the question is not only how to better regulate the police, but also how to think about the institutions that should step in before a situation becomes a police matter.
Comme les solutions institutionnelles se: If institutional solutions seem blocked or limited, what other paths can be proposed? On this subject, the evening’s participants were not short of solutions and voiced the main ideas driving the Quebec debate on policing.
Tout au long de la soirée, la colère de: Throughout the evening, the anger of Jean-Édouard Pierre-Toussaint, a community outreach worker in Côte-des-Neiges, stands in contrast to the calls for new reforms or new consultations. For him, the problem is not a lack of diagnosis. The reports exist, the recommendations pile up, and communities have long denounced racial profiling and police violence. “We’ve been asking for 40 years,” he says wearily. His criticism is aimed not only at institutions; it also challenges the strategy of asking for change from those who already hold power. “We have to stop asking,” he declares.
Derrière cette phrase se trouve une autr: Behind that sentence lies another way of envisioning change. Rather than waiting for a response from institutions, Jean-Édouard Pierre-Toussaint argues for more autonomy, more community organizing and a better balance of power.
Son intervention fait écho au sentiment: His remarks echo the feeling expressed earlier by Julian Grau-Brown, who said he felt that several generations keep passing down the same demands without ever seeing the hoped-for changes. For Mr. Pierre-Toussaint, the repetition of consultations, recommendations and promises itself contributes to the exhaustion of communities.
Sa position ne fait pas consensus dans l: His position is not a consensus in the room, but it reflects a need to break with the idea that institutions will inevitably end up correcting their own practices.
À la toute fin de la soirée, une discuss: At the very end of the evening, a discussion begins about the different ways to fight systemic racism. The exchanges reveal real disagreements. Some are betting on legal recourse or institutional reforms, while others favour a show of force, autonomy or a deeper questioning of the role of the police.
Pour Pierson Vaval, aucune approche ne p: For Pierson Vaval, no single approach can, on its own, transform a reality as complex as systemic racism. “The success or advancement of the community won’t come from action at just one level,” he says.
Invité à décliner la position de son org: Asked to spell out his organization’s position on a number of questions, the director of the Coalition Pozé refuses to set against each other the strategies that feed the anti-racist struggle. “You have to be an activist, you have to be a politician, you have to be in the system, you have to make money, you have to have influence, you have to be in the media… You have to be everywhere,” he argues.
Pour lui, la complémentarité des rôles d: For him, the complementarity of roles must be recognized: “You have to see the other person as an accomplice who may be fighting the fight where we can’t.”
À Anjou, les participants se sont largem: In Anjou, participants largely agreed on the diagnosis. Police racism is no longer seen as a succession of isolated incidents but as a systemic problem. The disagreements now have less to do with identifying the problem than with how to bring about change.
<strong>Définancer la police, une idée i: Defunding the police, an idea born of anti-racist movements
Popularisé aux États-Unis lors des manif: Popularized in the United States during the 2020 protests that followed the death of George Floyd, the slogan “Defund the police” refers to an approach that involves reducing police budgets in order to reinvest part of those resources in housing, mental health, education, prevention, community organizations and local services. Its supporters believe that several social problems are now handled by the police, when they are better addressed through social or community interventions.
À Montréal, la Coalition pour le définan: In Montréal, the Coalition pour le définancement de la police was created in 2020 and now brings together several dozen organizations. Among other things, it calls for a significant cut to the SPVM’s budget, reinvestment in neighbourhoods and the development of community-based safety solutions. According to an IPSOS poll commissioned by the City of Montréal in 2020, 73% of Montrealers said they were in favour of defunding the police. That direction was not taken up, however, by city hall, led at the time by Projet Montréal, which instead decided to increase the SPVM’s budget by 2%.
Quelles solutions au racisme policier à: What solutions to police racism in Montréal? Moratorium, commission of inquiry and defunding
Malgré des années de rapports et de reco: Despite years of reports and recommendations, solutions to police racism in Montréal struggle to be put into practice. Moratorium on police stops, public commission of inquiry, defunding the police and stronger oversight: researchers, legal experts and activists analyze the obstacles holding back reform.
